The two anchor questions

These guide every card discussion throughout the session.

Anchor question 1
What value might this behaviour bring to the team?
Anchor question 2
What constraint might this behaviour introduce in the way the team works?
Rule — After discussing both, the group decides: above or below the line. Nothing sits in the middle permanently.

Sorting prompts

Use sparingly during the sort. Silence is often more valuable.

"If we were at our best, what would we see more of?" "What would we see less of?" "Where do we agree? Where do we differ?" "Take your time — what is the value in this behaviour, even if it ends up below?" "Is this helping us get the results we want — or getting in the way?" "What would happen if we leaned more the other way?"
Debrief questions
Before we analyse anything — just notice. What actually happened in you? This debrief is personal before it is professional. Stay with the experience. Resist analysis.
"What surprised you about that conversation?"
"Was there a moment where something shifted — in yourself or in the room? Describe it."
"What did the cards make possible that a blank piece of paper would not have?"
"What happened when you held both questions — value and constraint — before deciding? Did that change anything?"
"Where did the conversation feel most honest?"
If the group is struggling

Tap any situation for the recommended response.

Slow the discussion before the dominant voice responds: "Before we hear from anyone else — take a moment. What's your own first reaction?"

Ask quieter participants directly by name.

Name what you see without blame: "I notice we've been building on one perspective — let's hear what's different."

Silence is System 2 thinking. Count to fifteen before considering any intervention.

The first person to speak after a genuine silence almost always says something worth hearing.

Filling silence prematurely is one of the most costly facilitation mistakes.

Name it directly: "I know some of you may not have chosen to be here. That's okay. I'm not here to tell you what good looks like — I genuinely don't know. That's your job."

Resistance drops fastest when people believe you have no agenda. Your restraint is the most credible signal you can give.

Do not fill it. Sit in it. Then: "That's an important observation. Can you say more?"

Let the team respond. Your role is to make it safe for the gap to be seen — not to resolve it.

This is often where the most valuable conversation in the whole session lives.

Use the science plainly: "Kahneman's work explains why the conversation is qualitatively different when there's no right or wrong answer. Thaler and Sunstein's nudge theory explains why designing the choice environment produces more genuine outcomes than instructing. Deci and Ryan's Self-Determination Theory explains why teams that define their own standards commit in a way that teams given standards never do. We just applied all three simultaneously."

Say it calmly. You do not need to win. You need to be credible.

Name the dynamic and redirect: "I want to make sure we stay with the behaviour on the card rather than specific situations."

If it escalates: "There's something important here that may need a different conversation. Can we park this card?"

Know the boundary of the methodology. You are not a mediator.

Ask each group to move clockwise: "Look at how this group sorted the cards. What's different from how you approached it?"

Set the tone: "Your job is not to fix or debate. Your job is to understand."

Then bring everyone together: "Having seen different perspectives, where do we want to land as a broader group?"

Practitioner repertoire

Exercises

Five named exercises plus the improvement cycle. Tap any exercise to see full instructions.

1
Foundation
The full sort
All 80 cards. Above or below the line. Always run first with any new group.
60–90 minAll 80 cardsMax 6 per group
Setup
  • Remove theme cards and set aside before dealing
  • Shuffle the 80 cards and deal one at a time around the table
  • Display the opening question and two anchor questions on a slide
  • Say nothing else — do not explain the cards
How it works
  • Taking turns, each person flips one card face up
  • Group discusses both anchor questions before deciding placement
  • Above or below — nothing permanently in the middle
  • Cards in the middle are a parking space, not a resting place
  • Every card must be placed before the exercise closes
Debrief questions
  • Which cards slowed you down most? What was happening?
  • Where did you agree quickly? What does that tell you?
  • Where did you disagree? What does that tell you?
  • If you could shift just two or three behaviours — which would make the biggest difference?
2
Diagnosis
The theme audit
Deep dive into one theme pair or one quadrant. Spectrum sort from "we do this well" to "we need focus here".
30–45 min10–20 cards
Options
  • Option A: Pull all 10 cards from one theme pair
  • Option B: Task quadrant (Goal Directed, Creative, Authentic, Confident)
  • Option C: People quadrant (Empowering, Supportive, Collaborative, Empathetic)
Spectrum sort
  • Cards sorted left to right: ← We do this well ... We need more focus here →
  • Extra anchor: "Where does this honestly sit for our team right now — not where we want to be, but where we actually are?"
3
Gap analysis
The pressure test
Where we sit normally vs where we drift under pressure. The gap between rounds is where real culture lives.
70 min15–20 priority cards
Round 1
  • "Place these cards where you honestly sit on a normal working day."
Round 2
  • "Now — same cards. Where do you drift when things get hard?"
Debrief questions
  • Which cards moved most between normal and pressure conditions?
  • What does that gap tell you about your culture risk?
  • What would need to change for the same cards to stay in the same place under pressure?
4
Leadership
The gap map
Leaders and teams sort independently. The cards with the biggest gap are the most valuable conversations.
90 min2 groups20–30 cards
Setup
  • Two groups — leaders and team members
  • Sort independently using the same cards without seeing each other's results
  • 30 min sorting · 30 min comparison · 30 min facilitated conversation
Debrief questions
  • Which cards show the biggest gap between what leaders see and what the team experiences?
  • What might explain that gap?
  • What would need to happen for both groups to see the same reality?
5
Action
The commitment stack
Convert insight into a specific tracked plan. Named owner, named timeframe, observable practice per card.
45–60 min3–5 priority cards
For each priority card
  • What does this behaviour look like when we are doing it well?
  • What currently gets in the way?
  • What one change would most move this behaviour forward?
Output format
  • Named owner and specific next action for each card by number
  • If-then plan: not "be more collaborative" but "when X happens, we will do Y"
  • Record card numbers — use them to anchor the next session
The improvement cycle

What happens between sessions is where culture actually changes.

1
Select
3–5 priority behaviours by card number. The ones that matter most right now.
2
Diagnose
How often does it show up? What conditions make it more or less likely? What is reinforcing the opposite?
3
Design
Small interventions. Remove sludge. Make the priority behaviour more likely to occur naturally.
4
Practice
Named owner. Named timeframe. If-then plan: "When X happens, we will do Y."
5
Return
Pull the same card numbers. Re-sort: where are we now? Progress or gap — both are valuable.
Facilitator reference

Guide

The model, the science, and how to talk about it. Tap any section to expand.

The quadrant model

The 80 cards cluster into four quadrants — two above the line, two below.

Getting things done
Goal Directed · Creative · Authentic · Confident
Treating people well
Empowering · Supportive · Collaborative · Empathetic
Defensive — control
Controlling · Competitive · Critical · Demanding
Defensive — comply
Dependent · Conventional · Validating · Fearful

Both below-the-line quadrants are driven by the same force — threat response. One expresses it through dominance. The other through appeasement. Neither is a character flaw — both are responses to environments that make defensive behaviour the path of least resistance.

This changes how you talk about below-the-line behaviour with a client team. It is never a moral judgement.

The behavioural science

Every element of the methodology maps to peer-reviewed research.

Kahneman — System 1 & System 2
The cards shift groups into slow, deliberate thinking. Holding cards, taking turns, and discussing both value and constraint are all System 2 triggers. The facilitator's restraint is the most important System 2 protection.
Thaler & Sunstein — Nudge theory
The facilitator is a choice architect. Every element — the question, the cards in hand, the turn structure, the above/below obligation — shapes the conversation without dictating its conclusion.
Deci & Ryan — Self-determination theory
Autonomy (I chose this) + Competence (I can do this) + Relatedness (we're in this together) = intrinsic commitment. The team decided the standards — not you. That's why they'll hold.
Cialdini — Social norms theory
Agreed standards, stated aloud in the room, become genuine social norms. Public commitment dramatically increases follow-through compared to private intention.
Schein, Duhigg, Kotter — Culture change
Most culture programmes fail because they operate at the artefact level. The cards work at the espoused values level. The improvement cycle works at the assumption level — changing the systems that reinforce current behaviour.
Facilitator as choice architect

Your job is to design an environment in which the team discovers its own answer — and owns it.

Do

Choose the right opening question before the session
Create conditions for safety — no judgement, no correct answer
Observe without intervening unnecessarily
Let silence breathe — count to fifteen before intervening
Reflect back what you hear without editorialising

Don't

Share your own view on any card or behaviour
Explain the numbers, colours, or themes during the sort
Direct the group toward a particular placement
Fill silence with commentary or suggestions
Summarise prematurely — let the team summarise

The hardest thing: most facilitators add value through contribution. This methodology asks you to add value through restraint. The structure and anchor questions do most of the facilitation work.

Positioning with clients

How you talk about this determines what doors open.

Language that closes doors

Culture workshop → Culture programme → Team building → Soft skills development

Language that opens doors

Behavioural standards framework → Team operating agreement → Facilitated behaviour design → Performance alignment tool

The one-minute explanation

"Most culture initiatives fail because they tell teams what the culture should be — and people comply without committing. Culture Science Cards flips that. Teams use a structured card-based process to define their own behavioural standards. Because they decide, they own it. The research on intrinsic motivation is clear: ownership produces commitment that instruction never does. The process takes 90 minutes. The outcome lasts."
